newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Competition forces Lane Crawford out of Singapore.
newsitem.headline: Competition forces Lane Crawford out of Singapore.

text.p: Hong Kong's Lane Crawford has become the latest victim of Singapore's retail slump, the fourth department store this year to announce it was closing its doors, analysts said on Tuesday.

Lane Crawford will pull down its shutters on Singapore's Orchard Road shopping highway for the last time at the end of this month, three years after opening and 12 months after halving its floor space in a vain effort to stem losses.
France's Galeries Lafayette was the first of this year's victims. Its Orchard Road store is now being converted into the latest edition of Planet Hollywood.
K-mart was next and Tanglin General Store shut up shop earlier this month.
Industry analysts said the closures pointed to a weak outlook for a retail sector plagued by high overheads and operators that cannot get their merchandise mix right.

"The Singapore retail scene is still very alive. But to succeed, you have to understand the market, and some stores are expanding even as others close," said Ong Choon Fah, director of research with real estate consultants Edmund Tie & Co.
She said demand for prime space along Orchard Road was still strong with no empty shops in sight. Rents for shops on the street level were still between Singapore $30-S$40 per sq ft.
"It is better to make a quick exit if you don't have the right formula rather than stay on," Ong said.
According to its landlord, Marco Polo Developments Ltd, a member of the same group, Lane Crawford wanted to decrease the size of its store again and become a "speciality store."

Marco Polo said it turned down the request, saying it feared Lane Crawford might not be able to meet rental payments and because it could make more in rent by dividing the property into smaller shops.
In the year ended March 1995, Lane Crawford's Singapore unit had a net loss of Singapore $36.4 million (US$26 million).
Marco Polo said Lane Crawford had told it that "further losses have been suffered and its trading has not improved since the downsizing exercise".
Lane Crawford is not alone. Almost all locally listed retailers have reported dismal results during the year.

Robinsons and Company, one of Singapore's oldest home-grown retailers, reported a dip in earnings for the first time in 10 years. It said net profit fell 10.8 percent to S$25.34 million in the year ending June 30, 1996.
CK Tang lost S$28 million last year while Metro Holdings saw net profits plunge 84.6 percent to S$1.08 million due to write-offs and the closure of its joint venture K-mart stores.

Isetan Singapore bucked the trend, returning to the black with a S$2.0 million profit after two years of losses. Analysts said Lane Crawford's problem was that its goods were too upmarket and the store was too dependent on tourists.

"Singapore is still a mass market when it comes to department store retailing. To survive here, you have to go for the domestic market," said Jennifer Chan, manager at Takashimaya department store on Orchard Road.
Chan said Takashimaya aims to make 70 percent of its sales to Singaporeans.
